problem: ROS 2 navigation stacks offer strong 3D SLAM but lack an integrated, modular pipeline that unifies perception, semantic representation and high-level reasoning online. Existing approaches rely on manual configuration or static class lists.
motivation: Robots in unfamiliar indoor environments must interpret high-level, context-dependent user intent (e.g. "I'm thirsty") and ground it to goals in the map. This requires a semantic map that is built online with open vocabulary and connected directly to navigation planning.
key_idea: A modular ROS 2 framework that continuously fuses SLAM, online open-vocabulary scene graph construction (VLM object descriptions, LLM-inferred spatial relations) and LLM reasoning to select navigation goals from ambiguous language requests.
insight: Coupling a dynamically built open-vocabulary scene graph with foundation-model reasoning lets a robot resolve indirect commands without static class lists or manual configuration. Only the abstract was available, so no ablations or quantitative analysis can be cited.
method: SLAM: the existing ROS 2 3D SLAM stack supplies the map and robot pose.
Dynamic open-vocabulary scene graph: VLMs describe detected objects online, and the graph is built continuously.
Relation inference: an LLM infers spatial relations between objects in the graph.
Language-guided goal selection: an LLM resolves ambiguous natural-language requests ("I'm thirsty", "I'm tired") against the scene graph to pick a navigation goal.
Navigation integration: the selected goal is passed to the ROS 2 navigation planner, all in a modular deployable pipeline.

setting.backbone: VLM + LLM foundation models (unspecified in the abstract)
setting.observation: RGB-D plus SLAM on a TurtleBot 4 (sensor details not given in the abstract)
setting.action_space: navigation goals passed to the ROS 2 planner (continuous velocity control)

results: Only qualitative demonstrations on a TurtleBot 4 in office environments are reported. NAIS handles high-level, context-dependent commands such as "I'm thirsty" or "I'm tired". No quantitative results or baselines are given in the abstract.
limitations: Evidence is limited to qualitative office demos, with no benchmark or quantitative evaluation in the abstract.
Depends on the latency and reliability of VLM/LLM calls for real-time operation, and the abstract does not address this.
